NCT of Delhi
20. The claims raised by the parties require further examination.
21. We propose to consider the same on the next date, i.e., 01 st
September, 2026 .
22. However, for the present, we grant liberty to the Delhi Government
to appoint candidates who have qualified in the DSSSB Examination, 2023
to fill up 581 sanctioned posts based on merit. Further, 32 posts in
pursuance of DSSSB Examination 2025 may also be filled up according to
merit.
15

## Page 93

23. We record the submission on behalf of the Delhi Government that 90
(contractual) special teachers have been screened by the Screening
Committee and found to be qualified. Also, 176 (contractual) special
teachers who had been screened by the Screening Committee constituted
by the Delhi Government shall be appointed in the TGT category on the
available vacant posts.
24. In the order dated 07 th March, 2025, passed by a co-ordinate Bench
of this Court, direction was given that special teachers who have already
been working and teaching for the “last many years” would be entitled to
have their candidature considered by the Screening Committee upon
relaxation of age limit in appropriate cases.
25. The phrase “last many years” has been interpreted differently by
different learned counsel appearing for the parties.
26. We have been referred to the parent decision of this Court [on the
subject of appointment of special teachers for Children with Special Needs
(CwSN)] in Rajneesh Pandey v. Union of India 1, where we do not find
any direction that the (contractual) special teachers appointed on contract
must have put in a particular duration of service in order to be eligible for
regularization.
27. Having regard to such state of affairs, the need has now arisen to
construe and define the phrase “for the last may years” to avoid future
complications.
28. We draw guidance from the decision in  Secretary,  State  of
Karnataka  &  Ors.  v.  Uma  Devi  &  Ors. 2 where in paragraph 53, the
Constitution Bench had observed regarding formulation of a scheme for
1  (2021) 17 SCC 12  (2006) 4 SCC 1
16

## Page 94

regularization of employees who had put in more than 10 (ten) years of
contractual /ad hoc service without judicial intervention, as a one-time
measure, and hold that those (contractual) special teachers who had put
in more than 10 years of service as on 07 th March, 2025 would only be
considered for regularization in service in terms of the order dated 07 th
March, 2025. The said order stands modified to this extent and, presently,
will be applicable for NCT of Delhi only, since the number of qualified
teachers outnumber the sanctioned posts.
29. Insofar as those teachers appointed on contract who fall short of the
mark of 10 (ten) years may participate in future examinations to be
conducted by the Delhi Government. We hope and trust that having
regard to the years of service put in by them (less than 10 years), some
weightage would be given to them.
30. We propose to take up the claims related to the State of Madhya
Pradesh, and the Union Territories of Lakshadweep, Ladakh and NCT of
Delhi on 01st September, 2026, at 03:00 p.m.

This  appeal  challenges  the  order  dated
20.03.2026 passed by the High Court of Punjab and
Haryana at Chandigarh in CRM-M No.72259 of 2025.
Apprehending arrest in connection with Crime
No.26/2025  registered  at  Police  Station  –  GRP
Hisar, District – GRP Ambala Cantt. for the offence
1

## Page 96

punishable under Sections 305(c) and 3(5) of the
Bharatiya  Nyaya  Sanhita,  2023,  the  appellant
preferred  an  application  before  the  High  Court
seeking anticipatory bail under Section 482 of the
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (“BNSS”
for short).
Said application for anticipatory bail has been
rejected by the High Court vide the impugned order
dated 20.03.2026. Hence, the instant appeal has
been preferred.
By order dated 20.04.2026, this Court issued
notice  to  the  respondent  and  directed  that  no
coercive  steps  shall  be  taken  against  the
appellant. 
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
and learned counsel for the State and perused the
material on record. 
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted
that pursuant to the interim protection granted by
this  Court,  the  appellant  has  joined  the
investigation and is cooperating with the same;
that  the  allegations  as  against  the  appellant
2

## Page 97

herein are not really true but he has been dragged
into criminal proceedings although he is innocent
and merely because co-accused Aryan disclosed his
name during the course of his investigation.  He
therefore, submitted that the impugned order may be
set aside and the appellant may be granted the
relief of anticipatory bail by making the interim
order absolute.
Per  contra ,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent/State,  with  reference  to  his  Status
Report submitted that the appellant is cooperating
with the investigation and hence appropriate order
may be made in this appeal. 
Taking note of the aforesaid submissions, we
hold that the appellant has made out a case for
grant of anticipatory bail and is entitled to the
relief claimed under Section 482 BNSS.
We, therefore, allow this appeal and set-aside
the order passed by the High Court. We direct that
in  the  event  of  arrest  of  the  appellant,  the
Arresting Officer shall release the appellant on
bail, subject to furnishing cash security of the
3

## Page 98

sum  of  Rs.25,000/-  (Rupees  Twenty-Five  Thousand
only) with two like sureties.
It is directed that the appellant shall extend
complete cooperation in the ensuing investigation.
The appellant shall not misuse his liberty and
shall not in any way influence the witnesses or
tamper with the material on record. 
Any infraction of the conditions may entail
cancellation of anticipatory bail granted to the
appellant.
With the aforesaid directions, the criminal
appeal is allowed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

 VERSUS

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. I.A. No.163222/2026 is allowed.
3. Heard the learned counsels appearing for both the
parties including the learned counsel appearing for the
intervenor.
4. The present matter arises from a dispute relating to
1

## Page 129

agricultural  land  between  close  relatives  regarding
possession and cultivation. The appellant alleges that the
complainant – Harbans and his family members were
attempting to forcibly retain and control over the land
belonging to the appellant’s branch of the family. According
to the appellant, on 22.01.2026, the complainant – Harbans
alongwith Premchand and Samandari, trespassed into the
appellant’s house, locked the house and assaulted him with
lathi, dumbell and knife and attempted to use country-
made pistol and he claims to have acted only in aid of his
private defense. Whereas in the complaint lodged in FIR
No.14/2026 (the present one) against the appellant, it is
alleged that the appellant herein attacked him with knife
and as a retaliatory and counterblast to FIR No.14/2026
lodged by complainant – Harbans, FIR No.15/2026 had
been registered. Apprehending his arrest, the application
for anticipatory bail was filed before the Sessions Court
which came to be rejected and the High Court also affirmed
the same on account of gravity of allegation and opining
custodial interrogation of appellant was warranted. 
2

## Page 130

5. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the
parties, we notice that there is no dispute with regard to
the fact that both the complainant and the appellant are
closely related. The dispute has arisen with reference to
the agriculture land.
6. Learned counsel appearing for the intervenor would
vehemently oppose grant of bail on the ground that
Harbans had sustained ten injuries on face, neck, shoulder
and it is his contention that he has received the telephonic
threat calls from appellant to withdraw the FIR and he
apprehends danger to his life.
7. Having regard to the relationship between the parties
and no material having been placed by the intervenor to
demonstrate that on receipt of such threat calls, any
complaint having been lodged, we are of the considered
view that appellant would be entitled for being released on
anticipatory bail. We also take note of the fact that in the
complaint lodged by the appellant which culminated in
registration  of  FIR  No.15/2026,  the  accused  persons,
namely, the complainant in FIR No.14/2026 and two others
3

## Page 131

have already been granted bail as an additional ground for
accepting the plea of the appellant in the instant case. It
would not be out of context to refer to the injuries
sustained by the appellant also which are seven in
numbers and it is the case of the appellant that on account
of the assault made by Harbans, who is the complainant in
FIR No.14/2026, he had sustained injuries. This would only
indicate that both the parties being relatives are fighting
for ownership of agricultural land and there being cross
FIRs are all facts which have persuaded us to grant the
relief.  Hence, for the reasons aforestated, we allow this
appeal, set aside the impugned order and direct that the
appellant  be  released  on  anticipatory  bail  by  the
jurisdictional Investigating Officer on such terms and
conditions including the condition of directing him to
appear on every Monday, Friday and Sunday between
11:00 a.m. to 01:00 p.m. and mark his attendance before
the  jurisdictional  police  and  cooperate  with  the
investigation and also on the condition that he shall appear
before the trial court on all the dates of hearing without fail
4

## Page 132

except  when  exempted  specifically  and  such  other
conditions as the Investigating Officer deems fit to impose. 
8. Pending application(s), if any, stands consigned to
records.

O R D E R
Heard learned counsels/senior counsel for the parties.
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeals arise out of the common impugned order
dated 23.10.2024 passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at
Bilaspur in  CRMP Nos.919, 964 and 1854 of 2018, by which the
petitions filed by the respondents have been allowed and the
petition filed by the appellant has been dismissed thereby, setting
aside the orders dated 07.03.2018 and 26.03.2016 passed by the
learned Additional Sessions Judge (FTC), Kabirdham, Chhattisgarh
and by the learned JMFC, Kabirdham, Chhattisgarh in Cr. Revision
No.15 of 2016 and 16 of 2016 and Criminal Case No.292 of 2016 and
quashed the criminal proceedings arising out of Criminal Case
No.292 of 2016 filed by the appellant against the respondents.  
4. Learned counsel for the appellant stated that a case was filed
by the respondents against the appellant in which, a medical report
was produced with certain findings recorded therein, which were
prejudicial to the appellant. It was submitted that the said
document was forged and fabricated and thus, the appellant had
filed a criminal complaint against the respondents under Section
195 read with Section 326/34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for
short, the “IPC”). However, the respondents being aggrieved, moved
before the Court of learned Additional Sessions Judge (FTC),
Kabirdham, Chhattisgarh against the very filing of the complaint on

## Page 137

3 
the ground that it was not maintainable as the bar of Section 195
of the erstwhile Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (for short, the
“Cr.P.C.”)  gives  protection  to  the  respondents  against  such
complaint. It was submitted that the High Court though has noticed
the settled law in terms of the Constitution Bench judgment of this
Court in Iqbal  Singh  Marwah  and  Another  v.  Meenakshi  Marwah  and
Another,  (2005)  4  SCC  370  but  has  without  explaining  the
distinction  held  that  the  facts  of  the  present  case  were
distinguishable and thus, benefit of the same could not be granted
to the appellant. It was submitted that the law, as settled by this
Court in Iqbal  Singh  Marwah  (supra), is crystalised in paragraph
no.33 of the said judgment. Learned counsel for the appellant
submitted that the document was created earlier in time i.e. prior
to filing of the complaint case by the respondents and the same was
used in the said petition. Thus, the two incidents are distinct and
separate. The first part relates to creation of a forged document
and the second part relates to presentation/relying upon the said
document for the purposes of maintaining a criminal case and using
it before the Criminal Court. Thus, it was submitted that as the
allegation  basically  related  to  creation  of  the  forged  and
fabricated document, the complaint could not be said to be not
maintainable.
5. Learned senior counsel for the respondents submitted that in
the case filed by the respondents, the appellant stands convicted
under Section 323/34 of the IPC vide order dated 29.08.2017 passed
by  the  learned  Judicial  Magistrate  First  Class,  Kabirdham,
Chhattisgarh and the document was not exhibited. However, there is

## Page 138

4 
no allegation with regard to the said document being used in the
other case.
6. At this juncture, on a direct query of the Court to the
learned senior counsel for the respondents as to under such
circumstances, all the more reason why the bar of Section 195 of
the  Cr.P.C.  would  not  apply,  learned  senior  counsel  fairly
submitted that in view of the judgment in  Iqbal  Singh  Marwah
(supra), strictly speaking, the complaint could not be said to be
not maintainable. However, he tried to persuade the Court that in
the facts and circumstances of the present case, the parties being
two senior Doctors, this acrimony ought to end.
7. Having considered the matters in their entirety, we find
substance in the contentions of learned counsel for the appellant.
On the short point of maintainability, we find that the High Court
has misdirected itself by failing to appreciate that in the facts
and circumstances of the present case, the ratio of this Court in
Iqbal Singh Marwah  (supra) is squarely applied. The complaint case
filed by the appellant against the respondents was maintainable and
it was open to the respondents to take all objections available
thereafter, during the said proceeding.
8. Accordingly, the appeals are allowed. The common impugned
order dated 23.10.2024 passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at
Bilaspur in CRMP Nos.919, 964 and 1854 of 2018 is set aside. The
complaint case filed by the appellant against the respondents is
held to be maintainable. However, the respondents are given liberty
to raise all their pleas and defences before the Court below.

CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION

DHANANJAYA SAHOO                    APPELLANT(S)
                       VERSUS
STATE OF ODISHA THROUGH SHO EOW, 
ODISHA, BHUBANESWAR  RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated
05.03.2026 passed by the High Court of Orissa
rejecting  the  regular  bail  prayer  of  the
appellant in connection with EOW, CID CB,
Bhubaneswar P.S. Case No.02/2025.
4. The submission of the learned counsel for
1

## Page 157

Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.10198/2026
the  appellant  is  that  the  crux  of  the
allegations against the appellant is of being
Managing Director of Companies which solicited
deposits  from  general  public  without  any
authority in law and under false promise of
doubling  the  amount  in  a  short  term  has
swindled the money and thereby cheated the
depositors.  Though it is also alleged that
forged documents like agreements, brochures
etc.  were  used  but  there  is  no  material
collected during the course of investigation
to indicate that those documents were false
documents within the meaning of Section 464 of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
5. In such circumstances, it is submitted
that  the  offences  alleged  to  have  been
committed by the appellant are all punishable
with a maximum sentence which may vary from 7
2

## Page 158

Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.10198/2026
years to 10 years.
6. It has also been submitted that though
maximum sentence under Banning of Unregulated
Deposit Schemes Act, 2019 is 10 years, the
minimum is 3 years. It is urged that since the
appellant by now has suffered about 1 ½ years
of incarceration and the trial is not likely
to conclude in near future as, according to
the charge-sheet, the investigation is still
pending  qua  other  accused,  though  already
three  have  been  indicted  including  the
appellant, it is a fit case that the appellant
may be released on bail on such terms and
conditions as the Court may deem fit to impose
in the facts of the case.
7. The learned counsel for the State has
opposed the prayer for bail by submitting that
the appellant is the kingpin of the entire
3

## Page 159

Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.10198/2026
fraud and, therefore, if he is released on
bail, he may abscond.
8. Having  regard  to  the  nature  of  the
offences alleged to have been committed by the
appellant and the fact that the appellant by
now  has  remained  in  jail  for  a  period
exceeding 1 year 6 months, and the trial is
not likely to conclude in near future, we are
of the view that the appellant is entitled to
be  released  on  bail,  pending  trial  on
stringent conditions.
9. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed. The
order passed by the High Court rejecting the
bail prayer of the appellant is set aside.
10. The  appellant  shall  be  released  on
stringent bail conditions to the satisfaction
of the Trial Court.  Amongst those conditions,
the following shall necessarily be there: (i)
4

## Page 160

Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.10198/2026
if the appellant has a valid passport, he
would be required to surrender the same; (ii)
he  shall  report  to  the  police  station
concerned where the First Information Report
was registered in the first week of every
month; (iii)  there shall be two sureties of
the sum of Rs.25 lacs each and those sureties
shall be solvent; and (iv) the appellant shall
submit his mobile number so that in case of
need he could be contacted/tracked.
11. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall
stand disposed of.

and those sureties shall be solvent; and

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Our Order dated 27th October, 2025 reads thus: 
“1. By our order dated 12.08.2025, we appointed Hon’ble Mr.
Justice Nageswara Rao, Former Judge of the Supreme Court of
India as the Ombudsman of the Bihar Cricket Association.
2. We requested the learned Ombudsman to have a formal meeting
with the stake holders and try to workout the modalities for the
smooth functioning of the Bihar Cricket Association.
3. It appears that after our order dated 12.08.2025, some
developments have taken place as pointed out by Mr. Rajiv
Shakdher,  the  learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
petitioner.
4. We have looked into the order passed by the learned Ombudsman
dated 26.09.2025 in BCA/Ombudsman/Complaint No.6/2025 and the
connected matters.
5. It appears that the learned Ombudsman is seized of the larger
issues involved between the parties and is looking into the
same. This is evident from the observations made in paragraph
‘21’ of the order passed by learned Ombudsman which reads as
under:
a) The BCA Amended Rules and Regulations, 2025 cannot be acted
upon till they were registered by the Registrar of Societies. 
b) No Rules of Procedures for conducting elections have been
made by the General Body in accordance with Rule 34 of the
Amended Rules and Regulations, 2025. 
c) The Resolutions dated 19.01.2025 and 25.05.2025 only relate
to eligibility of the office bearers of the BCA to contest the

## Page 177

3
election. They are not the Rules of Procedure as provided for in
Section 34 of the Amended Rules and Regulations, 2025 of the
BCA.
d) The Ombudsman has ample power to pass appropriate orders in
the Complaints filed before him. There is no restriction on the
types of disputes and differences that can be decided by the
Ombudsman.
e) The Electoral Officer is temporarily appointed to conduct the
elections, unlike the Ombudsman who holds office for a period of
one year at a time subject to maximum of three years.
f) The Electoral Officer has not been given the power to decide
the correctness of inclusion of persons in the voters’ list. 
g) The present Committee of Management illegally interfered with
the elected committee of the District Cricket Associations and
managed to have their own people being nominated from several
District Cricket Associations to become full members of the
BCA.” 
6. What we have been able to gather is that the petitioner has
serious grievances as regards the preparation of the electoral
roll and the conduct of the election of the Executive Committee
of the Association. 
7. The aforesaid aspects, more particularly, the legality and
validity of the electoral roll and the transparency in the
conduct of election etc. would be looked into by the Ombudsman.
8. We should wait for the appropriate report that the learned
Ombudsman may file in this regard. Once the report is before us,
we shall take an appropriate call in the matters.
9. List on 15.12.2025.”
2. In pursuance of our Order, referred to above, Hon’ble Mr.
Justice L. Nageswara Rao has forwarded his Report dated 26th
February, 2026. 
3. We looked into the Report, which is quite exhaustive. The
learned Ombudsman in the Ist part has given a brief introduction of
the proceedings, followed by an analysis of issues related to the
2025 BCA elections. The conclusion contained in Part III of the
Report reads thus:-
“84. As per the order of the Supreme Court of India, I confined
my inquiry to those matters which a direct bearing on the
composition of the electoral college for the election to COM,
BCA, September 2025 and the democratic functioning of the
association.
85. During the course of the hearings, I was apprised of several
critical issues affecting the governan of the BCA. Foremost
among them are the grievances concerning the constitution of
ad-ho committees and the purported non-adherence to the orders

## Page 178

4
passed by the Ombudsman.There serious allegations regarding the
arbitrary removal of elected office bearers of various DCAs,
violations of principles of natural justice. Upon a detailed
conspectus of the facts and the applicable rules, it was
observed that the administrative actions of the BCA deviated
from  the  established  procedure.  The  practice  of  summarily
removing elected bodies and appointing ad-hoo committees without
following due process, undermines the democratic fabric of the
association  Furthermore,  the  disregard  for  the  Ombudsman's
jurisdiction in matters of dispute redressal was found to be
contrary to the BCA Rules & Regulations.
86. A peculiar complaint that I came across was of Jehanabad
DCA, which adopted an odd interpretation of its bye-laws where
office bearers elected in bye-elections were granted a fresh,
full three-year tenure from their specific date of election,
rather  than  serving  only  the  remainder  of  the  existing
committee's unexpired term. This practice caused the tenures of
individual office bearers to expire at different intervals,
thereby preventing the simultaneous dissolution of the Committee
of Management and resulting in a perennial cycle of staggered
elections.
87. The detailed summaries of the complaints received and
examined during this inquiry are attached herewith as Annexure
A. Additionally, the various orders that I passed during the
course of the hearings are attached herewith as Annexure B.
88. In light of the aforesaid findings and to ensure the smooth
and lawful functioning of the BCA in the future, it seems
appropriate to propose few remedial measures. Accordingly, the
recommendations arising from this inquiry are set out in the
following section.”
4. The final recommendations as contained in Part IV read thus:-
“89.  Ombudsman:  The  BCA  R&R  stipulate  appointment  of  an
Ombudsman for a period of 1 year, which may be extended up to 3
years by the General Body, BCA. The minimum tenure of the
Ombudsman must be extended to 3 years, to ensure continuity in
functioning  and  consistency  in  adjudication.  The  present
provision providing for a term of 1 year is inadequate and
extension of the same would ensure security of tenure to the
Ombudsman.  Moreover,  a  provision  for  impeachment  may  be
included, requiring a resolution of the General Body, BCA by a
3/4th  majority  to  protect  the  Ombudsman's  tenure.
90.  Administrator:  Upon  examination  of  the  allegations
pertaining to DCA elections, I have sufficient reason to believe
that the electoral college requires a thorough reassessment. I
recommend that an Administrator be appointed by this Hon'ble
Court, who shall be tasked with conducting a verification
exercise across all DCAs, similar to the exercise undertaken in
2022 by the Ombudsman-appointed committee. It is imperative to
ensure that the electoral college only consists of valid member-
clubs and does not become a tool for proxy voting through
invalid clubs. Furthermore, any changes to the electoral college
in the future must be done strictly in accordance with the

## Page 179

5
constitution of the DCAs. In the event any club of a DCA is
sought to be removed from the electoral college, a proper notice
to such a club must be given, they must be given an opportunity
of being heard, and the decision should be subject to a
mechanism of challenge before the Ombudsman. Similarly, any new
affiliation to a club in a district, should also follow due
legal process stipulated in the articles of association/rules
and regulation of the concerned entity.
91. Fresh elections: Several discrepancies pertaining to the
electoral college have been enumerated above. In light thereof,
the elections of BCA conducted in 2025 cannot be deemed to
having  been  conducted  freely  and  fairly.  It  is  therefore
recommended that after the Administrator has completed his task
of verification of DCA clubs, the BCA's electoral college should
be recalibrated and elections to the DCAs and BCA should be
conducted in accordance with the rules and regulations governing
the BCA and the various DCAs.”
5. In Para 90 of the recommendations, referred to above, the learned
Ombudsman has suggested that an Administrator be appointed by this Court
who shall be tasked with conducting a verification exercise across all
DCAs, similar to the exercise undertaken in 2022 by the Ombudsman
appointed Committee.
6. In view of the aforesaid, we appoint Hon’ble Mr. Justice
Chakradhari Sharan Singh, former Chief Justice of the Orissa High
Court, to act as an Administrator of the Bihar Cricket Association.
7. The learned Administrator shall proceed further in accordance
with  what  has  been  recommended  by  the  learned  Ombudsman  as
contained in Paragraph 91 of the recommendations, referred to
above.
8. The fees of the learned Administrator and other modalities
shall be fixed in consultation with the parties. 
9. We are informed that there are some objections on record
insofar as the Report of the learned Ombudsman is concerned. We
shall look into the same at an appropriate time. 
10. As an interim measure, we direct that the recommendations
shall come into force forthwith and be implemented. 
11. We expect all the parties to cooperate and extend full
cooperation to the learned Administrator we have appointed today.
12. We have already appointed Hon’ble Mr. Justice Deepak Gupta,
former Judge of this Court as the Ombudsman of the Bihar Cricket

## Page 180

6
Association.
13. Post this matter on 8-10-2026 at 3.00 p.m.

IN

P. Sakthi & Ors. …. Petitioner

…. Alleged Contemnors/

O R D E R
The order of this Court dated 02.05.2025, which gave rise to
the contempt petition has been complied with. We need to state
briefly on the facts to dispose of the matter, though the petitioner’s
counsel also agrees that the order has been complied with.
2. Petitioner was before this Court aggrieved with the denial of his
claim, for consideration of his promotion to the post of Sub-Inspector
in the year 2019, when a notification was issued for considering
eligible constables for in service promotion in the 20% departmental
quota. Petitioner was denied participation in the selection quoting
the  punishment  imposed  on  him,  pursuant  to  a  disciplinary
proceeding by order dated 09.05.2005; despite the order having
been set aside, in an appeal, by order of the Government dated

## Page 188

27.11.2009.  We  directed  his  eligibility  to  be  considered  and
promoted from the year 2019 with all consequential benefits, since
it  was  not  his  fault  that  the  authority  denied  his  claim  for
consideration for promotion.
3. When  the  contempt  case  was  filed,  the  respondent-State
through  the  Additional  Chief  Secretary  to  Government  filed  an
affidavit contending that 20% in service quota is not a promotion but
a recruitment, where there is a regular selection procedure with a
written examination, which has to be qualified. It was also submitted
that  the  petitioner’s  case  will  be  considered  in  2027  selection;
especially  since  his  retrospective  appointment  in  the  year  2019
would unsettle the inter se seniority of the recruits in the selections
made in 2019, 2022, 2023 and 2025.
4. We were quite unhappy with the counter affidavit filed by the
State; especially since the said facts were never attempted to be
brought to the notice of this Court, when the matter was disposed of
nor was an attempt made to file a review from the order passed.
5. Be that as it may, we were quite sure in our mind that even if it
was brought to our notice, that in service quota was a recruitment
and not a promotion, we would have directed his case to be taken
up and considered on the basis of suitability as on the back date,

## Page 189

dehors the  circumstance  that  he  had  not  appeared  for  written
examination,  which  non-appearance  was  due  to  the  denial  of
participation by his superior authority. Hence, we summoned the
Additional Chief Secretary, who was the deponent to the affidavit,
finding contempt prima facie on the face of the affidavit. On the last
date of hearing, we gave an opportunity to the contemnors to purge
themselves of the contempt committed. 
6. Today,  an  affidavit  has  been  filed,  specifically  indicating
compliance, appointing the petitioner as a Sub-Inspector of Police
(Tamil Nadu Special Police) against the recruitment notified under
Notification  No.2  of  2019  w.e.f.  01.09.2021  and  the  seniority
conferred at the bottom of merit list of Sub Inspectors of Police
recruited pursuant to that notification. The Government order has
also been issued providing that the petitioner would be entitled to all
the consequential service benefits and such other benefits as are
admissible under the applicable rules. The Director General of Police
has also been directed by the Government to take further necessary
action and ensure compliance in the spirit of the order, to the last
letter.
7. We make it clear that the above order has been passed in the
peculiar facts and circumstances of the case, where the Government
and its Officers failed to reckon an Appellate Order having set-aside

## Page 190

the  punishment  imposed  while  declining  participation  in  a
recruitment of in-service candidates, especially when the Appellate
Order of the Government was passed long before the recruitment
itself.
8. We dispose of the contempt petition making it clear that if any
benefits are not actually granted to the petitioner as per the original
order in the civil appeal, the petitioner would be entitled to move
this Court.
9. Pending application(s), if any, also stand(s) disposed of

O R D E R
1) Leave granted.
2) The  appellants  seek  suspension  of  the
sentence imposed upon them during the pendency of
their appeals before the High Court challenging
their conviction for the offence punishable under
Section 3(1) of the U.P. Gangsters and Anti-Social
Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986.  They were
sentenced  to  undergo  ten  years  of  rigorous
imprisonment by the Trial Court.  Being aggrieved
1

## Page 208

by  the  rejection  of  their  applications  for
suspension of sentence by the High Court, the
appellants are before us.  
3) We have heard the learned counsel appearing
for the parties. 
4) Suffice it is to state that, no doubt, the
appellants have a number of criminal antecedents
but  the  fact  remains  that  they  have  already
undergone about six years of imprisonment out of
the total sentence of ten years and that the
sentence of the co-accused have been suspended and
they have been granted bail.  
5) In such view of the matter, we deem it
appropriate  to  set  aside  the  impugned  orders
passed by the High Court. Thus, the impugned
orders passed by the High Court stand set aside.
The sentences of the appellants stand suspended
and they are granted bail during the pendency of
their appeals before the High Court on such terms
and conditions as may be imposed by the concerned
Trial Court.  
6) Accordingly, the appeals stand allowed.

COL. MUKUL KUMAR GOGOI (RETD.)      RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. The appeal is directed against the judgment and
order  dated  11th September,  2015  passed  by  a  Division
Bench of the Gauhati High Court (the High Court of Assam,
Nagaland, Mizoram & Arunachal Pradesh) dismissing an intra
court  appeal1 of  the  appellants  and  thereby  refusing  to
interfere with the judgment and order dated 03 rd May, 2013
of  the  Single  Judge  passed  on  a  writ  petition 2 of  the
respondent.
2. We heard Mr. Puneet Taneja, learned senior counsel
1  WA No.58/2014
2   WP(C) No. 191/2013
1

## Page 213

for the appellants and Mr. Manish Goswami, learned senior
counsel for the respondent on previous occasions. We have
heard them today too.
3. The order dated 29th July, 2026 passed by us records
our prima facie satisfaction that the appellants do not have a
sound case. We reiterate such finding on the ground that the
appellants  had  terminated  the  respondent’s  service  on
probation in a manner which is in the teeth of the decision of
this Court in Dipti Prakash Banerjee Vs. Satvendra Nath
Bose National Centre for Basic Sciences, Calcutta3. The
impugned judgment and order is upheld.
4. Since, however, the respondent was appointed on
probation for a period of a year, effective from 01 st February,
2011 to 31st January, 2012 and such service came to be
terminated on 06 th June, 2011, we hold that he would be
entitled to the emoluments which he would have received
had he completed the period of probationary service during
the aforesaid period.
5. The last pay certificate of the respondent for May,
2011 has been placed before us. We, therefore, direct that
based on the emoluments so received by the respondent in
May, 2011, he shall be entitled to further emoluments at the
3  (1999) 3 SCC 60
2

## Page 214

same rate for the period 06 th June, 2011 to 31 st January,
2012 on the basis thereof.
6. A calculation sheet is also placed before us by Mr.
Taneja. It appears therefrom that the respondent would be
entitled  to  Rs.11,86,586/-  (Rupees  eleven lakh  eighty  six
thousand five hundred eighty six) only minus Rs.96,858/-
(Rupees ninety six thousand eight hundred fifty eight) only
(amount paid on 26 th March, 2014 in compliance with an
order  dated  28th February,  2014  of  the  Division  Bench),
which is equal to Rs.10,89,728/- (Rupees ten lakh eighty
nine thousand seven hundred twenty eight) only.
7. Let such amount of Rs.10,89,728/- with interest @
6% be paid to the respondent from the date of presentation
of  the  writ  petition  before  the  High  Court,  as  early  as
possible but not later than three months from date of receipt
of a copy of this order.
8. In the event the respondent has any dispute with
regard  to  the  quantum  of  money  payable  to  him,  as
aforesaid, he shall be free to approach the appropriate court
for relief, in accordance with law.
9. Prayer  of  Mr.  Goswami  that  this  Court  ought  to
consider the action of the appellants in refusing to grant a
certificate,  which  would  have  enabled  the  respondent  to
3

## Page 215

apply for future employment, for additional compensation is
considered and refused.
10. We further record the fair submission of Mr. Taneja
that whatever dues on account of Provident Fund for the
period  from  01st February,  2011  to  31 st May,  2011  are
payable to the respondent shall also be released within the
aforesaid period.
11. The  appeal  stands  disposed  of  on  the  aforesaid
terms.
12. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.

O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order  dated
13.10.2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad rejecting the regular bail prayer of the
appellant  in  connection  with  Case  No.  99/2021,
registered at P.S. Mirzamurad, District Varanasi.
4. The submission on behalf of the appellant is
that he was not named in the First Information
Report which was lodged against two unknown gunmen.
In  the  incident,  a  minor  girl  and  two  others
received  injuries.  The  appellant  came  to  be
implicated based on the statement of one Anil Yadav
1

## Page 223

who claimed himself to be an eyewitness. Another
witness, namely, Bhaiyalal, was set up to show a
prior  incident  to  prove  motive.  It  has  been
submitted  that  the  appellant  has  suffered
incarceration since 01.04.2021; the trial is nowhere
near conclusion; and the appellant has no previous
criminal antecedents; therefore, on being released
on bail, there is no likelihood of it being misused.
It has also been submitted that this is a case where
no test identification parade was conducted.   
5. The learned counsel for the State-respondent
has opposed the prayer for bail but could not
dispute that the trial would take some time to
conclude and the appellant has been in jail for a
period exceeding five years; and that he has no
previous criminal antecedents. 
6. Having regard to the submissions above, without
expressing any opinion on the merits of the case, we

released on bail at this stage.

passed by the High Court rejecting the regular bail

## Page 241

2. The  present  Special  Leave  Petition  calls  in
question the correctness of the order dated 27 th April,
2026  in  CRLMA(SOS)  No.  1/2026  in  Criminal  Appeal
No.2367/2022 passed by the High Court of Gujarat at
Ahmedabad. By the said order, the High Court has rejected
the prayer for suspension of sentence of the petitioner
pending hearing of his appeal. The petitioner has been
convicted for the offence punishable under Section 302 of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and was sentenced to undergo
life  imprisonment  and  fine  of  Rs.50,000/-  and  also
convicted under Section 30 of the Arms Act, 1959 with
simple imprisonment of six months and fine of Rs.2,000/-
and further convicted under Section 135 of the Gujarat
Police Act and sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment
of one year and fine of Rs.5,000/-.
3. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner
submits that the petitioner has already undergone 5 years
and 9 months in custody.  Learned counsel has also drawn
attention to the evidence of PW-13 to put forward a case
of private defence.  Learned counsel submits that in this
background the petitioner has a more than a reasonable
chance of acquittal.  Learned counsel further submits
that the parameters prescribed in the case of Omprakash
Sahni v.  Jai  Shankar  Chaudhary  And  Anr.  Etc. 1 are
attracted in favour of the petitioner.
1.(2023) 6 SCC 123
SLP (Criminal) No.12304/2026 Page 2 of 4

## Page 242

4. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
vehemently opposes the prayer for suspension of sentence.
Learned  counsel  submits  that  PW-13  was  wholly
untrustworthy.  Learned counsel further submits that no
injury was caused on the accused and the theory of self-
defence is itself completely untenable.  In any event,
the learned standing counsel submits that the petitioner
has far exceeded the right of private defence and fired
at the deceased on the head causing the death.
5. Having  considered  the  overall  facts  and
circumstances, having perused the evidence on record and
keeping in mind the period undergone as well as the
principles laid by this Court in Omprakash  Sahni’s case
(supra), we are inclined to suspend the sentence of the
petitioner and enlarge him  on bail, pending hearing of
the Criminal Appeal No.2367 of 2022 before the High
Court.
6. The sentence imposed on the petitioner is suspended
and the petitioner is directed to be enlarged on bail
subject to the satisfaction of the Trial Court, pending
disposal of the Criminal Appeal by the High Court.

CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).             OF 2026

MANISH KUMAR                                                          ...APPELLANT(S)

THE STATE OF BIHAR                                         …RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R 
1. Heard. Leave Granted.
2. The Appellant was arraigned as an accused in FIR No. 297 of 2025
registered for the offences punishable under Sections 191(1), 191(2), 190,
126(2), 115(2), 109, 352, 351(2), 351(3) of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
(in short  ‘BNS’) and Section 27 of the Arms Act, is seeking for being
enlarged on regular bail after such prayer made before the Trial Court and
the High Court as having been negatived.
1

## Page 281

3. Having heard the learned Advocates appearing for the parties, on perusal
of the counter affidavit emerged from the records that the allegation made
in the complaint is the effect that appellant and co-accused had arrived at
the informant’s house with firearms and lathis and it was alleged that
appellant fired at the informant namely Binod Kumar causing a gunshot
injury in left eye. 
4. The learned counsel appearing for the Appellant would contend that the
said FIR is counter blast to the attack initiated by the informant side and in
this regard, an FIR has been registered in FIR No.298 of 2025 by the
appellant’s family alleging that the informant side had attacked with sticks
and Binod Kumar had fired from country made pistol 6 to 7 times. Hence,
Appellant seeks for grant of regular bail.
5. Having heard the learned Advocates appearing for the parties, it would
emerge from the records that co-accused (have already been enlarged on
bail). Though there is a specific allegation of firing against the appellant,
the fact remains that, as per the averments made in the complaint that
other co-accused also had carried the firearms. Even according to the
prosecution there is no recovery of weapon from the appellant. Hence, we
are of the considered view that the Appellant is entitled for bail, released
on regular bail. The Appeal is allowed and the Impugned Order is hereby
set aside. The Appellant is ordered to be released on bail on such terms
and conditions as may be deemed fit and appropriate by the jurisdictional
2

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard Mr. T. N. Singh, learned counsel for the
petitioner; Ms. Sakshi Kakkar, learned counsel for the State of
Uttar Pradesh; and Mr. Shiv Charan Garg, learned counsel for
respondent Nos.6-11.
1

## Page 305

2. On 05.05.2026, this Court had passed the following order:
3. The petitioner approached the High Court
of Judicature of Allahabad, Uttar Pradesh
(High Court) with two grievances. The first
grievance was with regard to the appointment
of  Respondent  Nos.8  to  11  as  Assistant
Teacher  (Primary  Section)  attached  to
Intermediate College on the ground that the
said  respondents  did  not  possess  the
eligibility  qualification.  The  second
grievance of the petitioner is that the same
respondents have been promoted to the post of
Assistant Teacher (LT Grade), though they did
not have the eligibility criteria of TET
pass, which the petitioner possess.
4. While the High Court declined to interfere
qua the first grievance on the ground of
delay,  insofar  the  second  grievance  is
concerned,  the  High  Court  observed  that
Respondent Nos.8 to 11 may not possess the
essential qualification of TET pass.
5.  The  challenge  has  been  made  by  the
petitioner  without  delay.  However,
notwithstanding such observation, the High
Court relegated the petitioner to the forum
of Director of Education (Respondent No.2) to
canvas  his  grievance  viz-a-viz  Respondent
Nos.8 to 11, who was thereafter directed to
pass a reasoned and speaking order within two
months.
6. Prima facie, we are of the view that once
the High Court came to the conclusion that
challenge  to  the  promotion  of  Respondent
Nos.8 to 11 by the petitioner was without
delay and prima facie had merit, the High
2

## Page 306

Court ought to have examined this challenge
of the petitioner, instead of relegating the
petitioner before Respondent No.2.
3. Though respondent-State has filed counter affidavit, we are
not inclined to enter into an adjudication on merits in view of
what we have observed in para 6 of our order dated 05.05.2026, as
extracted supra. We are of the view that the High Court ought to
have examined the challenge instituted by the petitioner to the
promotion of respondent Nos.8-11 on its own merit. 
4. Accordingly, we set aside the order dated 13.01.2026 passed by
the High Court and remand the matter back to the Division Bench of
the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad by reviving Special
Appeal No.32/2026 which shall be heard now on its own merit and in
accordance with law, uninfluenced by any subsequent developments
that may have taken place pursuant to passing of the impugned order
by the High Court on 13.01.2026. We request the High Court to
expedite the hearing of the Special Appeal and dispose of the same
within a period of 6 months from the date of production of a copy
of this order.
5. Special Leave Petition is accordingly disposed of.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Application  for exemption  from filing  certified
copy of the impugned judgment is allowed.
2. Heard  Mr.  Neeraj  Kishan  Kaul,  learned  senior
counsel appearing for the petitioner.
1

## Page 314

3. Learned  senior  counsel  contends  that  the
petitioner-hotel has subscribed to the cable operator who
has  a  licence  from  the  respondent-Society.   Learned
senior counsel drawing attention to paragraphs 28 and 40
of the judgment of this Court in the case of  Hotel  &
Restaurant Assn & Another v. Star India (P) Ltd. & Others1
contends that the petitioner is not transmitting signals
to any other person. On the contrary, the petitioner is
recipient of it.
4. Learned senior counsel further drawing attention to
Section 52(1)(k) of the Copyright Act, 1957 submits that
the said sub-clause only deals with an ‘enclosed room
meant  for  common  use’  and  cannot  be  extended  to
individual rooms in a hotel which obviously are not for
common use purposes.
5. Learned  senior  counsel  also  distinguishes  the
judgment of the learned Single Judge of the Delhi High
Court in the case of Super Cassettes Industries Ltd.  v.
Nirula  Corner  House  (P)  Ltd. 2 inter  alia on the ground
that not only was the said judgment rendered in the
context of an Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil
Procedure, 1908 application but the said judgment did not
notice the judgment of this Court in Star India (supra).
1 . (2006) 13 SCC 753
2 . (2008) SCC OnLine Del 360
2

## Page 315

6.  Learned senior counsel submits that the Trial
Court had rightly declined the injunction and pending
appeal, the respondent did not have any interim order.
Learned  senior  counsel  submits  that  under  the
circumstances, to force the petitioner to seek a licence
from the respondent would be contrary to law.
 7. Issue notice, returnable on 12th October, 2026.
8. Till the next date of hearing, there shall be an
interim stay of operation of the impugned order.

1. An order of the High Court of Delhi rejecting the appellants’ plaint under
Order VII Rule 11, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (referring to the bar of the civil
court’s jurisdiction under Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the
pendency of a company petition 1 before the National Company Law Tribunal 2,
Bench at Allahabad) is under challenge in this appeal.
2. We are informed, in course of hearing, that two applications 3 have been
filed in connection with the company petition before the Tribunal seeking
dismissal thereof on the grounds urged therein. 
3. We are also informed that the applications have been heard on previous
occasions by the Tribunal and are due to be heard further on 24th August, 2026.
4. Since a decision on the applications might have some bearing on the issue
we are seized of, it would be in the interest of justice to adjourn hearing of this
civil appeal awaiting the Tribunal’s decision thereon.
5. The Tribunal may expedite its decision on the applications. Subject to its
convenience, it would be desirable if the applications are decided within a
month from date of conclusion of final hearing.
6. The resultant decision of the Tribunal, if rendered by the next date of

upon them to take care of their minor daughter - Mihira alias
Mahalakshmi, more particularly, when she needs some special care

“21. We are left with the observation
with which we began. Each of these parties
has come to us complaining of a wrong, and
each has been the author of a good part of

Court and this Court for eleven years. That

 UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. According to the prosecution, seven accused
persons namely Ram Mehar (petitioner), Ram Bhagat,
Rekha, Anita, Vikram, Milli (juvenile) and Illu,
formed  an  unlawful  assembly,  shared  a  common
intention  and  committed  the  murder  of  deceased
Sandeep.
2. There is a discrepancy in the FIR and in the
statement recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C. as to
the nature of the weapon the petitioner was carrying
at the time of the incident.
3. The petitioner is in jail since 19.02.2021.
Out  of  38  listed  prosecution  witnesses,  the
prosecution has examined only 23 witnesses, while 3
others have been dropped.
4. Considering the entire facts and circumstances
of  the  case,  we  are  inclined  to  release  the
petitioner on bail, in connection with FIR No. 38 of
2021 registered at Police Station – Kaithal Sadar,
District – Kaithal for offences punishable under
Sections 148, 149, 201, 302, 506 and 120-B of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 on such terms and conditions
as may be imposed by the Trial Court, subject to the
2

condition that the petitioner shall co-operate with
the trial.
5. Accordingly, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of.

dismissed for default and we are now concerned with the
restoration of petition under Section 34 of the A&C Act.

execution  proceedings  to  release  the  amount  with  accrued
interest, deposited by respondent no.1, which is lying in
deposit with the Registrar, Civil Court at Cuttack.

this Court to mediate the dispute between the parties.

Mediator, shall be discussed in consultation with the learned
Mediator.

take the matter forward.

1. The  Union  of  India,  including  the  learned  Attorney
General for India, have held several meetings to find out a viable
solution to the pending execution proceedings for giving effect to
the judgment rendered by this Court on 27.09.2011 in State of
Himachal Pradesh vs. Union of India & Ors.,  whereby the suit filed
by  the  State  of  Himachal  Pradesh  was  decreed  in  part.  A
comprehensive note has been placed on record by the learned
Attorney  General  for  India  laying  down  the  modalities  for
implementation/execution  of  the  decree.  The  proposal  set  out
therein is acceptable in entirety to the State of Himachal Pradesh
as well as the State of Haryana. However, the State of Punjab has
some reservations on certain factual issues for which the said
State is permitted to submit its note by the next date of hearing.
2. Post the matter for further hearing on 24.08.2026.

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIPUL M. PANCHOLI
For Petitioner(s) :Ms. Uttara Babbar, Sr. Adv.
                   Ms. Sadhana Sandhu, AOR

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2.  Having heard Ms.Uttara Babbar, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
petitioner, we are not inclined to entertain this petition, which seeks to assail
the order of conviction. 
1

## Page 726

3.  However, we notice that the sentence of 20 years imprisonment that had
been imposed by the trial court was by application of amended provision of
Section 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO)
and same has been rightly interfered by the High Court by noticing that the
incident had occurred prior to the amendment came into effect i.e., on January,
2019 and reducing the sentence to 10 years. The amendment to Section 6 of
POCSO Act came into force wef 16.08.2019. Even under the unamended
provision of Section 6 of the POCSO Act the sentence that could have been
imposed was not less than 10 years imprisonment, which may extend to
imprisonment for life. The High Court by altering the sentence has not assigned
any reason as to why even in such heinous crimes, the imprisonment for life has
not been imposed or the accused has not been sentenced to life imprisonment.
In other words no reasoning has been assigned.
4. Hence, for considering as to why the sentence imposed by the trial court and
modified by the High Court, should not to be enhanced, we issue notice to the
petitioner, returnable in six weeks.
5. Let notice be served through jurisdictional Superintendent of Jail since
appellant-accused is undergoing the sentence imposed on him.
(RASHI GUPTA)                              (AJEET SINGH TARIYAL)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             BRANCH OFFICER

We   have  heard learned senior counsel and learned 
counsel appearing for the respective parties at length. 
During  the course of submission, it was brought to our 
notice that already 100 out of 349 witnesses have been  
examined and possibly the number of witnesses to be examined 
may be reduced by the prosecution. 
Having regard to the progress of the trial in Sessions 
Case No.256/2025 arising out of FIR No.18/2025 before the  
Exclusive Fast Track Sessions Court, Kamrup Metro, Guwahati, 
Assam, at this stage, we do not find any reason to direct 
transfer of the said proceedings to the Court of District and 
Sessions Judge, Patiala House Court, New Delhi as sought for 
by the petitioner herein.
Hence, the Transfer Petition is dismissed.
Pending  application(s)  shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The parties are already before the Supreme Court Mediation
Centre. The mediation proceedings are in progress.
2. What we have been able to gather in the course of today's
hearing is that the parties would like to put an end to their
marriage. However, the husband seems to be reluctant to pay
anything  to  his  wife  and  minor  son  towards  their  lifetime
maintenance. We made ourselves clear that we shall dissolve the
marriage subject to the husband offering a reasonable amount to his
wife and minor son towards full and final settlement. 
3. The learned Mediator shall now proceed in this direction and
persuade the parties to put an end to the entire dispute.
4. The Supreme Court Mediation Centre is requested to give a
Report to this Court as expeditiously as possible.
5. List the matter immediately after the Mediation Report is
received.
6. In the meantime, the further proceedings arising from the
First Information Report No.0770/2025 dated 3-7-2025 registered
with Police Station – Indirapuram, Ghaziabad, U.P. by the wife
shall remain stayed. We say so because the parties are already
before the Mediation Centre.

Ms. Simran Parmar, Adv. 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner-organisation seeks a direction under Article 32
of the Constitution to the Election Commission of India (ECI) and
other authorities to adopt the year 1993 as the cut-off year of
intensive revision. Notably, 2002 has been marked as the year for
Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in Sikkim and other States in the
Union of India. 
2. As such, it appears that the ECI has adopted a uniform year on
a pan-India basis.  That being essentially a policy decision
against which no political party or other stakeholders from the
1

## Page 798

State of Sikkim have come forward to oppose, we do not find it a
case warranting judicial review by this Court.  
3. We have heard learned senior counsel on behalf of the ECI
also, and he informed us that necessary steps based upon 2002 as
the cut-off year had already been taken in the State of Sikkim
also. Notably, it is not in dispute that SIR has taken place in the
State of Sikkim in the year 2002. In such circumstances, we find no
good ground to interfere with the fixation of the cut-off year.
The petitioner-organisation may, if so advised, pursue the matter
with the concerned authorities.
4. The Writ Petition is, accordingly, disposed of with pending
application(s), if any.
(NITIN TALREJA)                           (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR
